title: Subsystem Spacetime Code
authors: Esther Xiaozhen Fu, Aranya Chakraborty, Daniel Gottesman
abstract: Quantum error-correcting codes provide a powerful framework for analyzing and designing fault-tolerant Clifford circuits. In this work, we construct the subsystem spacetime code and use it to characterize the distances of Clifford circuits. We show that its gauge group can be explicitly constructed and classified using the masking properties of the instantaneous stabilizer groups and consists precisely of faults that are harmless to the circuit. We use this framework to identify where a dynamical code loses distance and to analyze how the fault distance changes when circuits are composed from smaller components. Our results provide a versatile tool for analyzing and designing fault-tolerant circuits, with potential applications to the construction of new dynamical codes.
summary: This paper introduces the subsystem spacetime code to analyze fault tolerance in complex quantum circuits. It constructs the code's gauge group by analyzing how stabilizer information is masked and propagated through time. The resulting framework successfully equates the code's distance to the circuit's true fault distance, offering a powerful diagnostic tool for designing robust quantum computation protocols.
main_problem: The paper aims to develop an algebraic framework to characterize the fault distance of fault-tolerant quantum circuits, particularly those involving complex dynamical processes where static code approaches fail.
main_result: The authors construct the subsystem spacetime code, proving that its gauge group structure explicitly characterizes the circuit's fault distance, providing a versatile tool for designing fault-tolerant circuits.
method: The methodology involves constructing the subsystem spacetime code and characterizing its gauge group using the masking properties of instantaneous stabilizer groups within a spacetime Pauli space formalism.
model_or_system: The model is quantum computation circuits involving Clifford gates and Pauli measurements, analyzed using a 'dynamical code' approach that tracks the evolution of the stabilizer group over imaginary time slices.
key_observables: Fault Distance, Gauge Group structure, Unmasked Distance ($d_U$), Measurement Error Distance ($d_{	ext{meas}}$), and the center of the gauge group.
important_parameters: The circuit composition structure, the type of fault model (e.g., measurement errors), and the specific Pauli operators defining the stabilizers.
main_assumptions: The framework builds upon prior work and assumes the circuit blocks are ideal; relating spacetime distance to unmasked distance requires a 'correctability condition'.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the key components of the subsystem spacetime code, detailing the basis for generators derived from detector stabilizers, gauge qubits, and commuting propagators.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by reviewing background theory, introducing masking properties and spacetime Paulis, specifying applicable circuits, constructing the gauge group and distance, relating distance to unmasked distances, and finally applying the framework to dynamical codes and circuit composition.
why_interesting: While focused on abstract QEC theory, the development of dynamical codes and spacetime structures provides powerful mathematical tools for analyzing error propagation in time-dependent quantum systems, which has parallels in open quantum systems dynamics.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Key ingredients of the subsystem spacetime code. The detector stabilizers Sdet form the center of G and are its stabilizers. Every other generator belongs to a gauge qubit: a pair of operators that anticommute with each other and commute with every other pair. Unmasked stabilizers, taken modulo Sdet, pair with commuting propagators across adjacent cuts; temporarily and permanently masked stabilizers pair with their destabilizers at the same cut; and adjacent logical generators pair with each other. Figure 2: The circuit model considered in this paper. We consider imaginary time slices through the circuit that separates successive operations. Each intermediate circuit block consists of unitary operations and measurements having disjoint supports.

Figure 3: Spacetime code structure for the Hastings and Haah’s Floquet code. (Left) A stabilizer in the spacetime code with weight 24. (Right) Each entry X, Y, Z denotes a weight-6 Pauli on a hexagon of the same Pauli type in the honeycomb lattice. Operators on the same column are supported by the same hexagon but at different timeslices.

Figure 4: Evolution of the distance-algorithm data. The left and right tracks show the states of Cj and Vj, respectively, after each measurement. The central nodes identify the measurement and the corresponding update rule.

Figure 5: Representing a measurement error on adjacent cuts. (a) The reported outcome of mea- suring m = Z1Z2 is flipped. (b) Two equivalent representations are X(t) 1 X(t+1) 1 and X(t) 2 X(t+1) 2 : the Pauli before the measurement flips its outcome, while the Pauli afterward cancels the residual data error. Thus, a single measurement fault admits non-unique representations of spacetime Pauli weight two.
